chapman_bristol.text: Chapbooks, shipshape and a little bit damp. Pay up, I run a tight ship. Like, a ship.

bristol_l.text: Listen for the Bristol L. Bristolians add an L to words that end in a vowel. An idea becomes an ideal; the area is an areal.
Some say the city's own name caught it. Bristol was once Brycgstow, Old English for the place at the bridge. Then Bristow. Then, well, Bristol.

rail_guard.text: Bristol Temple Meads! Brunel's station for his Great Western Railway, from London to Bristol, opened in 1840 and 1841.
All aboard! Trains to everywhere you've been. Mind the gap, and mind the man with the bike.

brs_dockhand.text: They call it the Floating Harbour because the water's kept in behind lock gates, so the ships float even when the tide's out.
Before 1809 ships here sat on the mud twice a day at low tide. Built 'shipshape and Bristol fashion', they had to be, to take it.

brs_cider.text: Ooh arr! No, nobody says that. Not really. Well, I do, but only after my second cider.
Where's it to? That's Bristolian for 'where is it?'. And when you get off the bus you say 'cheers, drive'. Manners, see.

brs_student.text: The Wills Memorial Building up Park Street is the university. Built with tobacco money, by the Wills family, in the 1920s.
Bristol's chocolate too: J. S. Fry and Sons made the first chocolate bar you could eat, here, in 1847. Science, that is.

brs_market.text: St Nick's! Pies, falafel, vintage records, a man who'll fix your watch and a woman who'll read your palm. Sometimes it's the same stall.
The Corn Exchange was built in 1743. Them bronze pillars outside are the Nails. Pay on the nail, my lover.

brs_fox.text: Bristol's famous for its urban foxes. Scientists at the university have studied them for decades, garden by garden.
They curl up on shed roofs in the sun. Absolute bin-raiding menaces. I love them.

brs_gromit.text: I work at one of the animation studios. Bristol's a big place for wildlife films and stop-motion. Plasticine everywhere.
Twenty-four frames a second. A week's work for a few seconds of a dog raising an eyebrow. Worth it.

then.text: Isambard Kingdom Brunel: bridges, tunnels, railways, ships. Died at 53. Did more than most would in three lifetimes.
Two stamps! The bridge and the ship. Last page is right here: Temple Meads, his station.
He designed the whole line from London, the Great Western Railway, with this old station at the Bristol end. One last question.
Prudence's question: why did Brunel use a broad gauge?
Exactly! Seven feet and a quarter of an inch between the rails. Wider track, steadier carriages, higher speeds.
He was right, too. It just lost the argument: most lines were already narrower. In 1892 the whole Great Western was changed over in one weekend.
Here. You've earned the notebook, and a little friend from the engine sheds who's been following me about all week.

else.text: Not quite. Think of the trains themselves. Have another go.

then.text: First page: the Clifton Suspension Bridge, up the Avon Gorge. Then the SS Great Britain, at the harbour. Then back here.

else.text: Brunel! Isambard Kingdom Brunel! Greatest engineer Britain ever had. I've found a copy of his notebook. Well, a facsimile.
Fancy following his trail? The bridge, the ship and this very station. Get each page stamped and come back.
Prudence hands you a battered copy of Brunel's notebook.

then.text: Another new piece went up on Picton Street last night. Nobody saw a thing. They never do.
Four new pieces round Stokes Croft and St Pauls. Find them all and come back to me.
You found all four AND met the painter? Nobody meets the painter! Here, from the gallery. Keep it quiet.

else.text: All four! Brilliant. Now, the painter always comes back to check on new work. Tonight, round the back of Jamaica Street.
Don't ask their name. Just... say hello. They like a challenge.
Someone's been painting again. Four new pieces overnight, all signed with a little spray can. Nobody knows who.
Fancy a treasure hunt? Find all four round Stokes Croft and Picton Street, take a good look, and come and tell me.

then.text: Crew's ready when Gwen is. Gloves on, hats on, and nobody hold on to the rope when she lifts.
Gwen wants a ground crew? We're the best in Bristol. But we only work for someone who can beat me. Ready?
Right, crew! Up to Ashton Court! We'll meet you at Gwen's basket.

else.text: Balloon crew, us. We hold the ropes, fill the envelope with a big fan and chase the balloon across Somerset in a van.
Best job in the world. Worst job in a hedge.

art_gull.text: Painted on the wall: a huge herring gull in a flat cap, sneaking a chip off a sleeping pigeon.
Underneath, in neat little letters: 'BRISTOL FASHION'.

else.text: You make a note of it for Saffron. (Piece 1 of 4.)

art_falcon.text: Painted on the wall: a peregrine in a top hat and tails, diving on a startled pigeon over a tiny bridge.
Someone's tagged it 'IKB WOZ ERE'. Brunel would have been delighted.

else.text: You make a note of it for Saffron. (Piece 2 of 4.)

art_tide.text: Painted on the wall: a giant tide gauge with sea creatures climbing it, the numbers going up to 14 metres.
A note says the Severn's tide is one of the highest in the world. Art, with a fact attached.

else.text: You make a note of it for Saffron. (Piece 3 of 4.)

art_balloon.text: Painted on the wall: a hot-air balloon made of apples, carrying a cow, a goat and a very surprised vicar.
It's signed with a little stencil of a spray can. Nobody knows whose.

else.text: You make a note of it for Saffron. (Piece 4 of 4.)

then.text: When you look back, there's only a fresh stencil of a spray can on the wall, still wet.

else.text: Not now. Come back after dark.
